title: Edge Threshold and Long Cycle Predicates
content: Four definitions build the formal framework. edgeThreshold(n,k) = C(n-k-1,2) + C(k+2,2) + 1 is the Erdős edge density threshold — the number of edges in the extremal graph K_{k+2} ∨ K_{n-k-2} (complete bipartite join). hasCycleOfLength checks for a cycle of exact length l using an injective vertex sequence with consecutive adjacencies (modular arithmetic for the closing edge). hasLongCycle is the universal statement: every n-vertex graph above the threshold has an (n-k)-cycle.
mathContext: $\operatorname{edgeThreshold}(n,k) = \binom{n-k-1}{2} + \binom{k+2}{2} + 1$. This equals the edge count of $K_{k+2} \vee \overline{K_{n-k-2}}$ (a clique of size $k+2$ plus an independent set of size $n-k-2$, with all cross-edges). This is the extremal graph: maximum edges without an $(n-k)$-cycle.

title: The Function f(k): Exact Values by Cases
content: The function f is defined directly by its known exact values: f(0) = f(1) = 1 and f(k+2) = 2(k+2)+3 = 2k+7. This is a noncomputable definition only in principle; the three cases are concrete natural numbers computable by pattern matching. The key theorem f_ge_two shows the Woodall formula: f(k) = 2k+3 for k ≥ 2. The alternative form f_ge_two_alt rewrites this as 2k+7 (using the shift by 2). Concrete values f(2)=7, f(3)=9, f(4)=11, f(5)=13 are immediately derivable.
mathContext: $f(k) = \begin{cases} 1 & k \in \{0, 1\} \\ 2k+3 & k \geq 2 \end{cases}$. This is the minimum $n_0$ such that every $n$-vertex graph with $\geq \operatorname{edgeThreshold}(n,k)$ edges has an $(n-k)$-cycle, for all $n \geq n_0$.

title: Four Axioms: Ore, Bondy, Woodall Upper and Lower Bounds
content: Four landmark theorems are axiomatized. Ore's theorem (1961): every graph on n ≥ 1 vertices above the threshold has a Hamiltonian cycle (the k=0 case). Bondy's theorem (1971): every graph on n ≥ 1 vertices above the threshold has an (n-1)-cycle (k=1 case), and in fact such graphs are pancyclic. Woodall's upper bound (1972): for n ≥ 2k+3, the threshold guarantees an (n-k)-cycle for any k. Woodall's lower bound: for k ≥ 2, n=2k+2 is too small — extremal graphs at n=2k+2 have no (k+2)-cycle. Together these four axioms pin down f(k) exactly.
mathContext: Ore (1961): $\forall n \geq 1, \operatorname{hasLongCycle}(n, 0)$. Bondy (1971): $\forall n \geq 1, \operatorname{hasLongCycle}(n, 1)$. Woodall (1972): $n \geq 2k+3 \Rightarrow \operatorname{hasLongCycle}(n,k)$ [upper bound]. Lower bound: $k \geq 2 \Rightarrow \neg\operatorname{hasLongCycle}(2k+2, k)$. The lower bound uses explicit extremal graphs: $K_{k+2} \cup K_{k}$ achieves the edge threshold without an $(k+2)$-cycle.

title: Correctness and Growth Rate: Combining Axioms into f(k)
content: The proved theorems derive f(k)'s properties from the axioms. f_is_upper_bound: by case analysis on k (using Lean's match), reduce to the appropriate axiom. f_tight: f(k)-1 fails for k ≥ 2, proved by showing 2k+3-1 = 2k+2 and applying the Woodall lower bound. Growth rate: f is strictly increasing for k ≥ 1 (2-step increase for k ≥ 2), linearly bounded by 2k+3, and at least 1. The cycle_length_at_boundary theorem shows the cycle length at n = f(k) is k+3 — the first 'interesting' cycle beyond the trivial triangle (k+2 > k+2... wait, k+3 for k≥2 means a (k+3)-cycle in a (2k+3)-vertex graph).
mathContext: $f$ is the minimum threshold: $\forall n \geq f(k), \operatorname{hasLongCycle}(n,k)$ and $\neg\operatorname{hasLongCycle}(f(k)-1, k)$ for $k \geq 2$. Growth: $f(k+1) - f(k) = 2$ for $k \geq 2$, giving an arithmetic progression $7, 9, 11, 13, \ldots$ At the boundary $n = f(k) = 2k+3$: the cycle length is $n-k = k+3$.

title: Threshold Symmetry at the Woodall Boundary
content: A key structural insight: at the Woodall boundary n = 2k+3, the threshold is symmetric — both binomial terms C(n-k-1,2) and C(k+2,2) equal C(k+2,2), making the threshold 2·C(k+2,2)+1. This is because n-k-1 = 2k+3-k-1 = k+2, the same as the second argument. The threshold difference between n=2k+3 and n=2k+2 is C(k+2,2) - C(k+1,2) = k+1. Concrete boundary values are computed by decide: threshold(3,0)=3, threshold(5,1)=7, threshold(7,2)=13, threshold(9,3)=21, threshold(11,4)=31.
mathContext: At $n = 2k+3$: $\operatorname{edgeThreshold}(2k+3, k) = \binom{k+2}{2} + \binom{k+2}{2} + 1 = 2\binom{k+2}{2}+1$. The symmetry $n-k-1 = k+2$ is the reason this is the Woodall boundary — it's the balanced point where both halves of the extremal graph have the same size. The sequence $3, 7, 13, 21, 31, \ldots$ follows the pattern $\binom{k+2}{2} \cdot 2 + 1$.

title: The Ore-Bondy Anomaly: f(0)=f(1)=1
content: For k=0 and k=1, f(k)=1 — the threshold works for ALL n ≥ 1, not just large n. This is anomalous compared to k ≥ 2 where f(k) = 2k+3 ≥ 7. The k=0 threshold simplifies to C(n-1,2)+2 (Ore's Hamiltonian condition) and k=1 to C(n-2,2)+4. These are exactly the conditions in Ore's and Bondy's original theorems. The jump from f(1)=1 to f(2)=7 (a gap of 6) is by far the largest relative jump in the sequence, reflecting a phase transition in the difficulty of the problem.
mathContext: For $k=0$: $\operatorname{edgeThreshold}(n,0) = \binom{n-1}{2}+2$, which corresponds to Ore's condition $\sum \deg(v) \geq n^2/2$ for Hamiltonian cycles. For $k=1$: $\operatorname{edgeThreshold}(n,1) = \binom{n-2}{2}+4$ for $n \geq 2$. The anomaly $f(0)=f(1)=1$ reflects that Ore/Bondy work for all sufficiently large $n$ (without a lower threshold on $n$), while Woodall needs $n \geq 2k+3$.
